MUSC.01.note: The tuning overview explains why fixed-pitch instruments need temperament, how equal divisions make every key usable, and what interval purity is sacrificed.

exercise.prompt: Calculate a pure 3:2 fifth and a twelve-tone-equal-tempered fifth from the same starting frequency, then measure the discrepancy in cents across a circle of fifths.

MUSC.02.note: UNSW's music-acoustics material connects periodic vibration, fundamentals, integer-multiple partials, resonance and instrument timbre using audible examples.

exercise.prompt: Synthesize one fundamental plus its first eight harmonics, change their amplitudes, and describe how the perceived timbre changes while pitch stays constant.

MUSC.03.note: The cross-cultural study finds both shared and culture-specific emotional cues, showing that the Western major-happy/minor-sad association is real for many listeners but not a universal acoustic law.

article.title: Harmonic Organisation Conveys Both Universal and Culture-Specific Cues for Emotional Expression in Music

exercise.prompt: Create matched major and minor versions of one melody, vary tempo and timbre independently, and ask listeners which feature most changes perceived emotion.

MUSC.04.note: Open Music Theory develops species counterpoint as simultaneous independent melodies and then connects those constraints to imitation and fugal writing.

exercise.prompt: Write eight bars of first-species two-voice counterpoint, checking melodic independence, consonance, contrary motion, voice crossing and treatment of perfect intervals.

MUSC.05.note: The digital-audio course explains timbre, spectra, masking and reconstruction, providing the foundation for missing fundamentals and other psychoacoustic effects.

article.title: Digital Audio
article.source: University of California, Irvine — Christopher Dobrian

exercise.prompt: Remove the fundamental from a harmonic complex, compare perceived pitch with a spectrogram, then create a repeating Shepard-tone sequence and explain the octave ambiguity.

MUSC.06.note: UCI's Max cookbook gives a concrete account of attack, decay, sustain and release as a control signal used to shape amplitude and other synthesis parameters.

article.title: ADSR Amplitude Envelope
article.source: University of California, Irvine — Max Cookbook

exercise.prompt: Build one oscillator into a filter and ADSR envelope, then make plucked, bowed, brass-like and pad-like presets by changing only waveform, cutoff and envelope timing.

MUSC.07.note: The Library of Congress recording-registry essay documents Gregory Coleman's six-second break and its extraordinary afterlife across sampling, hip-hop, jungle and electronic music.

article.title: Amen, Brother — The Winstons
article.source: Library of Congress National Recording Registry

exercise.prompt: Slice one drum break into hits, rearrange it at three tempos, and document how chopping, pitch, time-stretching and layering turn the same recording into different rhythmic vocabularies.

MUSC.08.note: Roland's history explains the 808's analog voice circuits, sequencer, commercial failure, discontinuation and later adoption across hip-hop, techno and pop.

exercise.prompt: Program a sixteen-step pattern using kick, snare, clap and hi-hat, then alter decay, tuning, accents and swing to hear why the machine behaves like an instrument rather than a static sample bank.

MUSC.09.note: Antares' official history connects Andy Hildebrand's geophysical signal-processing work to real-time pitch detection, correction and the deliberately audible zero-retune-speed effect.

article.title: About AutoTune: Voice Technology and History

exercise.prompt: Process the same vocal with slow, medium and zero retune speed, then compare pitch accuracy, transitions, vibrato, naturalness and the stylised hard-tuned effect.

MUSC.10.note: The University of Iowa demonstration frames hall design through reverberation, absorption, reflections, clarity and the trade-off between warmth and intelligibility.

article.title: Concert Hall Acoustics
article.source: University of Iowa Department of Physics and Astronomy

exercise.prompt: Estimate reverberation time for two rooms using volume and absorption, then predict effects on intimacy, clarity, bass warmth, speech and orchestral blend.

MUSC.11.note: Open Music Theory treats meter as interacting pulse layers, providing the foundation for hearing and notating cross-rhythm and polyrhythmic structures.

exercise.prompt: Clap a 3:2 and then a 4:3 polyrhythm, place both rhythms on a shared subdivision grid, and identify the points where attacks coincide.

MUSC.12.note: EBU R 128 explains the industry shift from peak normalization toward measured programme loudness, true-peak limits and loudness range, which reduces the reward for mastering everything louder.

article.title: Loudness Normalisation and Permitted Maximum Level of Audio Signals

exercise.prompt: Create two masters with different compression and limiting but loudness-normalize them to the same LUFS value, then compare punch, fatigue, transients and loudness range.
